While contrastive pretraining performs better on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet in low-data regimes, DiffPT is particularly effective on medical imaging and time-series tasks, where it outperforms self-supervised baselines across a range of low-data regimes. Our results suggest that DiffPT is a simple and effective approach for data-efficient classifier pretraining on different modalities.

title: TAN: A Size- and Form-Adaptive Masked-Convolution Encoder for Tissue Graphs
abstract: Tissue graphs represent histology images as graphs over tissue-conforming superpixels, which keeps homogeneous tissue regions intact instead of cutting them into rectangular patches. To embed superpixels, current encoders crop them to bounding boxes and then pad, resize, or mask them, so background or fill values can leak into the node features. This matters in practice, and especially in medical imaging, where a prediction should depend on the tissue and not on an arbitrary preprocessing choice: on BACH, changing only the fill of the masked region shifts the accuracy of frozen encoders by up to 6 percentage points, larger than the differences among the four best encoders under mean fill, and the preferred fill differs between datasets, so it cannot be fixed once and for all. We present TAN (Tissue-Aware Network), a compact convolutional encoder (0.41M parameters) that processes each superpixel at its native shape and extent and excludes background from every operation, which makes its embeddings exactly invariant to the fill by construction. Under identical masks and an identical graph classifier, TAN's accuracy on BACH is not significantly different from that of the 303M-parameter foundation model UNI (81.1% vs. 80.7-82.6%, depending on the fill), with ~740x fewer parameters, ~1,190x fewer FLOPs, and no pretraining. On BRACS, TAN is close to a ResNet18 trained under the same protocol and trails the histopathology foundation models. An ablation with TAN's architecture but standard processing of fill-padded crops shows that masking keeps accuracy similar (nominally higher on BACH, lower on BRACS, within noise) at less than half the FLOPs.

title: From Adult Renal Masses to Pediatric Wilms Tumors: Evaluating Cross-Domain Generalization of Kidney Lesion Segmentation on MRI
abstract: Deep learning segmentation models for pediatric oncology are often trained on small, single-center cohorts, whereas much larger datasets exist for adult diseases, such as kidney cancer. Whether models trained on adult renal lesions generalize to pediatric Wilms tumors remains unclear. We trained a segmentation model on single-sequence T1- or T2-weighted adult kidney MRI and evaluated it on a held-out adult test set and a pediatric Wilms tumor cohort, where it was compared with a pediatric-specific nnU-Net. Segmentation performance was quantified using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance. On the adult test set, the model achieved a median DSC of 0.86 for renal lesions. On the pediatric cohort, the adult-trained model achieved a median DSC of 0.85 compared with 0.90 for the pediatric-specific model. Despite differences in age, anatomy, and tumor type, the adult-trained model showed promising performance on pediatric Wilms tumors, with only a modest difference in median DSC compared with the pediatric-specific model. However, non-inferiority could not be shown, highlighting the value of pediatric training data. In future work, a fine-tuning strategy could be explored.

title: Enhancing RAG-based Medical VQA with Gated Multimodal Representations
abstract: Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) have shown strong performance in Medical Visual Question Answering (MVQA), yet they may still produce factually inconsistent responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can mitigate this issue by incorporating external clinical evidence; however, retrieval is often guided by a single modality, potentially overlooking the joint semantics of medical images and clinical questions. We introduce a multimodal RAG framework that learns a joint query representation through a Gated Multimodal Unit, enabling evidence retrieval to leverage information from both modalities while keeping the underlying Med-LVLM frozen. We evaluate the proposed approach on benchmark datasets. Results show that the multimodal query representation consistently outperforms a reference Med-LVLM and remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods. Our findings demonstrate the potential of multimodal query representations for more effective evidence retrieval in Medical VQA.

title: Beyond Multi-Stage Pipelines: A Label-Correlation Ensemble for Multi-Label Retinal Fundus Disease Classification
abstract: Retinal fundus images frequently carry more than one disease, and public fundus datasets are heterogeneous and severely long-tailed. Clinical triage suggests a staged design, in which a screening gate, a disease-group router and group-specific classifiers operate in sequence, but it is unclear whether this hierarchy earns its complexity. We present a controlled comparison of three architectures on a unified 39-target label space built from RFMiD 1.0, RFMiD 2.0 and ODIR-5K (12,652 images): (i) a three-stage gated cascade of eight models, (ii) a flat model with 39 independent sigmoid outputs, and (iii) a label-correlation model that replaces the flat linear head with 39 learned label queries and a two-layer transformer decoder. All three share one Swin-V2-B backbone, one preprocessing pipeline and one training protocol, so differences are attributable to the architecture. Staging offers no consistent advantage: tracing every missed disease instance to the stage that lost it shows that the two coarse gates discard 34.2% of true instances while the fine-grained classifiers lose only 6.7%, and the gates' hard zeros depress the cascade's macro-AUC to 0.747. Label-correlation modeling gives the largest single gain, raising the detection rate from 0.621 to 0.682 (0.689 with test-time augmentation). Blending the flat and label-correlation models under four-view test-time augmentation is the best configuration on six of eight metrics (exact match 0.694, micro-F1 0.678, macro-F1 0.456, macro-AUC 0.972). On definition-matched class subsets it matches or exceeds four recent studies on macro- and micro-F1, most clearly on low-support pathologies. We also show that ensembling a gated cascade with continuous-output models is harmful, and that per-source negative sampling is needed to remove a dataset shortcut that otherwise yields a spurious AUC of 1.000.

title: DinoMUSE: A DINOv2-guided Framework for Unsupervised Lateral Motion Estimation in Ultrasound Elastography
abstract: Quasi-static ultrasound elastography (USE) is a non-invasive imaging method for assessing soft tissue mechanical properties. Limited by low resolution, low sampling frequency and lack of phase information in the lateral direction, accurate lateral motion estimation remains a critical bottleneck in USE. Existing methods mainly rely on local image matching and physical constraints (such as tissue incompressibility assumption and effective Poisson's ratio), which lack sufficient contextual information. We present DinoMUSE, a DINO-guided mixture-of-experts (MoE) framework for unsupervised lateral motion estimation in USE. DinoMUSE incorporates high-level visual representations learned by DINOv2 into the motion estimation network to provide global contextual guidance. To facilitate effective interaction between DINOv2 features and local matching features, an MoE-based feature-fusion module adaptively transforms and integrates the two representations. Evaluations against NCC, GLUE, RAFT, and sPICTURE on simulation and in-vivo breast datasets show that DinoMUSE substantially improves lateral estimation accuracy while maintaining competitive axial performance. Specifically, DinoMUSE reduces the mean square error (MSE) of lateral displacement and strain estimation by 60% and 65%, respectively, compared with a SOTA algorithm on the simulation dataset. For in-vivo breast data, DinoMUSE achieves axial strain SNR and CNR of 5.70 and 4.82, and lateral strain SNR and CNR of 4.61 and 2.23, compared to 4.11 and 3.32, and 4.57 and 2.13 for the best competing method, alongside improved lesion visualization. These findings indicate the potential of leveraging transferable visual representations and adaptive feature fusion to improve lateral motion estimation in USE. The code is available at xxxxxxxx.

title: Implicit Neural Models for Direct Multi-Shell Diffusion MRI Signal Estimation
abstract: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging is a noninvasive technique that is sensitive to the motion of water molecules in human tissue. The image signal is commonly described in q-space; however, a complete coverage of this space is often infeasible due to hardware and acquisition time limitations. In this work, we propose to represent the entire diffusion signal using an implicit neural representation network with wavelet activation functions. The signal space is encoded using Fourier features and spherical harmonics basis functions for a continuous output distribution of the raw diffusion data, enabling both super-resolution and q-space interpolation. Additionally, we introduce a pretraining strategy using a group template, enabling faster per-subject optimisation when combined with nonlinear registrations of subjects into template space. We tested the method with 10 subjects from the Human Connectome Project and 26 subjects from in-house data (multidimensional diffusion MRI from a Parkinson's disease cohort). The results show that the proposed method yields high-fidelity reconstructions with significantly reduced memory requirements compared to raw diffusion-weighted images. The pretraining scheme showed good generalisability properties on data acquired with very different protocols. We further assess the method on downstream metrics relevant to diffusion MRI data from the learned representations.

title: Benchmarking and Improvement of Artifact Segmentation Methods in H&E-Stained Whole Slide Imaging
abstract: Technical artifacts introduced during tissue preparation or slide scanning remain a major obstacle to developing robust computational pathology algorithms for hematoxylin and eosin (HE)-stained whole-slide images (WSIs). Despite the growing number of quality-control tools, their real-world utility remains hard to assess because of the limited number of publicly available implementations and the lack of systematic, multi-dataset comparisons. This paper presents a benchmark of artifact segmentation methods for HE-stained WSIs. After a literature review, six publicly available algorithms were selected and compared in terms of their ability to segment artifact-free tissue and selected artifact classes. Two publicly available datasets and a newly introduced dataset released to support further research were used for evaluation. Tissue samples from multiple medical centers and different organs are included, enabling evaluation across heterogeneous data sources. Segmentation performance was assessed using Dice Index, pixel-level recall, and false discovery rate for artifact-free tissue segmentation. For algorithms supporting multiclass artifact segmentation, class-wise Dice Index and inter-class misclassification were evaluated. In addition to segmentation quality, processing time was assessed. Statistical analysis revealed significant differences in segmentation performance between methods. HistoKit, which incorporates a modified version of the GrandQC, was identified as the best-performing algorithm, while HistoQC was the worst. In terms of artifact types, dark spots and out of focus regions were harder to segment than others. Finally, a simple post-processing step was introduced for HistoKit, which further improved segmentation performance. The benchmark establishes a reference for evaluating and developing artifact segmentation methods for HE-stained WSIs.

title: GliomaINK: A Tumor and Anatomy Conditioned Flow Matching Framework for 3D MRI Sequence Synthesis in Glioma Patients
abstract: Background: Incomplete multiparametric MR examinations limit glioma characterization and downstream AI tools. Generative models can synthesize missing MRI sequences, but anatomical structure and clinically relevant tumor features are challenging to preserve. We propose GliomaINK, an anatomy-guided conditional flow matching framework for cross-sequence 3D brain MRI synthesis. Methods: A 3D SwinUNETR predicted the conditional velocity field while an auxiliary topology-preserving loss encouraged structural consistency. The model was trained on 1,083 patients from the BraTS-AG dataset and independently tested on an in-house clinical cohort. Downstream tasks include image quality, tumor segmentation, IDH1 mutation-status prediction, and overall survival prediction. Two radiologists independently evaluated the anatomical fidelity, pathological representation, and overall image quality of the synthesized images. Results: GliomaINK exhibited the highest PSNR across all six MRI translation directions in both evaluation cohorts. In the BraTS-AG test set, the PSNR reached $25.64\pm0.55$ dB for the T2W-to-T1C synthesis, compared with $13.78\pm0.32$ dB for Pix2Pix and $18.90\pm0.53$ dB for SPADE. For downstream tumor segmentation, the method showed strong performance across tumor subregions with Dice scores reaching $0.928\pm0.014$ for edema, and $0.885\pm0.040$ for enhancing tumor. For the IDH1 mutation-status prediction, GliomaINK achieved the highest AUROC score in four of the six sequence configurations, reaching $0.827\pm0.088$. Conclusion: Anatomy-guided conditional flow matching enables high-fidelity cross-sequence glioma MRI synthesis demonstrating potential for preservation of clinically relevant information in synthesized MRI and improving downstream tasks.

title: LUMINR: Intensity-conditioned Meta-learned INRs for Accelerated Medical Image Registration
abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) have been applied to deformable image registration, where a lightweight network maps a spatial coordinate to a deformation vector. Because an INR encodes one specific signal in its parameters, a fresh network must be optimized for every image pair at test time, which is slow. Existing methods reduce this cost by meta-learning an initialization across a population of image pairs, and condition the weights of the INR globally, so the same conditioning applies at every coordinate while the deformation field it initializes varies across the domain. We propose LUMINR, a meta-learning framework that accelerates this per-pair fitting and in which the conditioning is local instead. LUMINR uses an INR that maps a coordinate, together with local intensity and gradient features, to a deformation vector, so the conditioning varies over the domain at the resolution of the field being modelled. Its objective is to find an initialization of the INR parameters from which the network can be fine-tuned to register any unseen pair in only a few optimization iterations. We evaluate LUMINR on 3D deformable registration of brain MRI from the OASIS dataset, where local conditioning and the meta-learned initialization prove complementary: early in fitting they reach a markedly higher accuracy than either does alone. Fine-tuned from that initialization, LUMINR matches the accuracy of the same conditioned INR fit from scratch in roughly a tenth of the gradient steps and a tenth of the wall-clock time, while the deformation fields stay smooth with negligible folding.

title: NV-Generate-Body: 3D Latent Diffusion Model forControllable Anatomy, Tumor, and Demographic Body Mask Synthesis
abstract: Curating large labeled CT datasets is expensive and constrained by patient privacy. We present NV-Generate-BodyMask, a 3D latent diffusion model that synthesizes whole-body CT segmentation masks with precise, joint control over organ anatomy, tumor burden, and patient demographics. The model operates in the compressed latent space of a frozen mask autoencoder, generating $256^3$ volumetric label maps conditioned on a 19-dimensional vector via Adaptive Group Normalization and cross-attention. A size-adaptive ROI loss with spatial halo weighting and a paired tumor injection pipeline enable accurate tumor size conditioning despite the scarcity of annotated tumor cases. Trained on 8,571 masks across 26 cohorts spanning 132 labels, the model achieves Spearman $ρ= 0.70$--$0.92$ for organ size, 85--100\% tumor recall for lung, pancreatic, colon, and bone lesions, and strong demographic alignment (BMI $ρ= 0.78$, sex-conditioned perfect prostate control).

title: Landmark-Free and Scale-Blind Multi-View Registration of Preoperative Liver Models to Intraoperative Surfaces
abstract: Augmented-reality guidance in laparoscopic liver resection requires aligning preoperative 3D liver models from CT/MRI with intraoperative surfaces. Monocular reconstruction in most cases cannot guarantee scale, albeit rigid-motion registration requires scale as an input. Our proposed framework ``SimCompose'' estimates the full similarity transformation $\Sim$, including scale, without relying on landmarks and applies the same transformation across multiple views with known relative geometry. However, reliable detection of registration failures remains challenging in surgical settings, where ground-truth alignment is generally unavailable. For this, we propose a geometry-based selector that evaluates candidate transformations without requiring ground truth. Large disagreement among these transformations is used to flag potentially unreliable registrations. Finally, we propose to use a non-rigid refinement based on a low-dimensional deformation model from Neo-Hookean simulations in the Simulation Open Framework Architecture (SOFA), without additional network training. SimCompose is trained exclusively on synthetic partial views. Its encoder processes point clouds normalised to a unit root-mean-square radius, without access to metric scale, and filters each view before multi-view fusion. Evaluation on unseen synthetic data (300 single-view pairs per run; 100 three-view registrations) shows that multi-view integration and candidate selection increase the success rate under stringent $\Sim$ accuracy criteria from 38.4% for a single-view, single-method configuration to 77%. Existing learning-based baselines do not satisfy these criteria even when provided with the exact scale. On five in-vivo patients with 92 keyframes, the rigid registration stage reduces surface error more than three-fold relative to learning-based baselines with external scale information.

title: Enzyme-Activatable Probe for Tumor Bimodal Imaging, Intraoperative Navigation, and Urinalysis.
abstract: We develope an enzyme-activatable platform (NO 2 -RGD-Gd) for the integrated urinary biomarker detection, highcontrast fluorescence-magnetic resonance (MR) dualmodal imaging, and real-time image-guided surgical navigation within a single molecule. The advantages, including the favorable tumor-targeting affinity (RGD peptide), high renal clearance efficiency, and tumor-specific fluorescence activation, are achieved by rationally engineering the molecular architecture. Benefiting from these characteristics, the NO 2 -RGD-Gd effectively bridges the boundary between diagnosis and therapy, achieving outstanding combinatorial performance in in vivo applications. It allows early and precise diagnosis through urinary biomarkers, provides anatomical-pathological and molecular imaging information of tumor lesions via fluorescence-MR dual-modal imaging, and delineates tumor boundaries for accurate surgical navigation relying on tumor-targeted activatable fluorescence imaging signals. Furthermore, all these processes can be realized simply via intravenous injection, offering a more efficient and feasible strategy for integrated diagnostic and therapeutic applications.

title: Ocular morphology and morphometry of the great egret (Ardea alba): A comprehensive anatomical description.
abstract: Ardea alba (Linnaeus, 1758) is widely distributed, yet knowledge of its ocular morphology remains limited. This study described the morphometry and morphology of the eyeball and its accessory glands in six specimens using radiography, morphometry, light and scanning electron microscopy, and 3D scanning. The eyeballs showed similar descriptive morphometric values in the right and left eyes, accounting for approximately 11.2% of head mass and 12.12% of total skull length. The eye was classified as the flat type, a morphology previously associated in the literature with diurnal birds, featuring a yellow iris and a circular pupil. The scleral ring consists of 14 bilateral type A ossicles associated with hyaline scleral cartilage. Histologically, the cornea showed a well-defined Bowman's membrane, and the retina had 10 distinct layers. The pleated type pecten emerged from the optic nerve and extended toward the vitreous body. The accessory glands were characterized as follows: the Harderian gland (type II) was the most developed; the lacrimal gland was "hockey-stick" shaped; and the nasal gland (salt gland) was supraorbital in location and pyramidal in appearance. These results provide a robust anatomical basis for comparative avian ophthalmology.

title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Does Not Accurately Estimate the Size of Glenoid Labrum Tears in Patients With Shoulder Instability.
abstract: Purpose To compare magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based measurements of glenoid labral tears with intraoperative measurements. Methods A retrospective review was performed of patients that underwent shoulder capsulorrhaphy between 2019 and 2024 at a single academic medical center. All patients with a single labrum tear, an MRI within 6 months of surgery, and historical tear measurements or measurable intraoperative photographs were included in the study. Glenoid labrum tear size was noted using the clockface convention described in "hours." When clockface measurements were not reported on MRI reads, measurements were made by a radiologist. When clockface measurements were not reported in operative notes, measurements were made by an orthopaedic surgeon using intraoperative photographs. A paired t test was used to evaluate any difference between the MRI and intraoperative measurements. Results Two hundred sixteen glenoid labral tears from 211 patients met inclusion criteria. Average age was 27.2 ± 11.8 years, 68.5% of patients were men, and 56.9% of glenoid labrum tears were right-sided. On average, MRI measurements exceeded intraoperative measurements (4.15 ± 2.90 hours vs 2.80 ± 1.59 hours) with an average difference of 1.36 ± 3.09 hours (95% confidence interval = 0.94-1.77, P < .001) and a correlation of 0.154 ( P = .023). A greater difference in measurement was observed among men compared with women (1.64 vs 0.74 hours, P = .044). Conclusions MRI overestimated glenoid labrum tear size compared with intraoperative measurements and differed substantially between the 2 modalities on a case-by-case basis, with men displaying a larger discrepancy in measurement difference than women. These findings indicate that MRI may be more appropriately used as a categorical tool for confirming the presence of glenoid labral tears, rather than as a precise measure of tear size. Level of evidence Level III, retrospective diagnostic case series.

title: Spontaneous Bilateral Vesical Artery Pseudoaneurysms Presenting With Massive Recurrent Hematuria and Obstructive Acute Kidney Injury: A Case Report.
abstract: Spontaneous development of vesical artery pseudoaneurysm (VA-PA) as a cause of life-threatening hematuria is very rare. Most of the existing reports are due to trauma or other types of pelvic surgeries/urological procedures. Incomplete hemostasis in these patients can lead to subsequent complications such as clot retention, severe blood loss resulting in anemia and obstructive AKI. We report this extremely rare case of a 35 year old lady with bilateral VA-PA causing recurrent episodes of massive hematuria and obstructive AKI that was ultimately resolved by selective embolization. A 35-year-old female presented with a history of gross hematuria along with clot retention and severe anemia. She also had signs of obstructive AKI which required her to have temporary dialysis. Cystoscopy showed intravesical clot but no bleed site was identified on initial evaluation. On contrast-enhanced CT scan, there were pseudoaneurysms found from both sides coming off from left superior and right inferior branches of vesical artery. Following confirmation by selective pelvic angiogram, we did a superselective embolization using micro coils and PVOH particles to occlude both pseudoaneurysms. This resulted in immediate cessation of hematuria, normalization of renal functions and stabilization of Hb values. At last follow-up done in 6 weeks' time, all symptoms had resolved and there was complete thrombosis of both the lesions seen on imaging. Bilateral spontaneous vesical artery pseudoaneurysm is a condition that must be suspected in a patient presenting with recurrent episodes of severe hematuria despite having undergone seemingly successful endoscopic treatment. Immediate imaging of the vessels and selective angioembolization is the surest means of diagnosis and treatment, thus avoiding further complications.

title: Giant Cavernous Hemangioma in the Mesentery of the Descending Colon: A Case Report.
abstract: Gastrointestinal hemangiomas are rare, and those involving the mesentery are even more infrequent. The majority of cases reported in the literature had mesenteric cavernous hemangioma of the small intestine. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first documented case of a hemangioma originating from the mesentery of the descending colon. Preoperative diagnosis is exceedingly difficult, and various imaging modalities may be inconclusive. The patient was a 71-year-old Asian male presenting with recurrent dizziness and fatigue over several months. Physical examination revealed a mass that was palpable in the left mid-abdominal region. Laboratory examinations suggested gastrointestinal bleeding and anemia. Abdominal CT scans revealed a large mesenteric mass in the descending colon. The mass was surgically resected, and histopathological examination confirmed mesenteric cavernous hemangioma. The patient showed no signs of recurrence in 1 year of postoperative follow-up.

title: Reversal of refractory epilepsy in an adult with GAMT deficiency: A case report and comparative literature review.
abstract: Objective Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive creatine biosynthesis disorder. Reports specifically focusing on adult patients remain scarce. Methods We report a 52-year-old female (the oldest documented case of GAMT deficiency to date) presenting with severe intellectual disability, refractory epilepsy, and adult-onset disease progression. Whole-exome sequencing identified novel compound heterozygous GAMT variants (c.265_267del and c.253G>T), and magnetic resonance spectroscopy confirmed cerebral creatine depletion. Remarkably, initiating oral creatine supplementation at age 52 achieved complete seizure freedom, normalization of the electroencephalogram (EEG), and significant motor function recovery. Results A comprehensive review revealed that untreated adult patients face a high risk of progressive neurological deterioration. Compared to the pediatric cohort, adults exhibited a significantly higher prevalence of movement disorders (69.2% vs. 33.1%, p < 0.001) and a trend toward a higher prevalence of epilepsy (92.3% vs. 74.2%). Especially, atonic seizures (drop attacks) are particularly characteristic of adult GAMT deficiency, with EEGs frequently demonstrating background slowing, multifocal epileptiform discharges, and electrodecremental patterns. Significance This study underscores that continuous disease progression and prolonged neurotoxicity still could compromise the well-being of adult GAMT deficiency patients. Accurate diagnosis is essential for adults presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) phenotype, as even late treatment for GAMT deficiency can still dramatically alleviate the epileptic burden and reverse motor decline. Plain language summary We report the oldest known adult diagnosed with GAMT deficiency. Our case demonstrates that starting creatine treatment even at age 52 can dramatically reduce seizures and restore motor function. Literature shows that untreated adults suffer from more severe epilepsy and movement disorders than children, with symptoms worsening over time. These findings highlight the critical need for genetic testing in adults with unexplained severe epilepsy; timely creatine supplementation can halt cognitive decline and significantly restore quality of life.

title: Non-invasive diagnosis of endometriosis: From expert imaging to molecular and artificial intelligence-enabled pathways.
abstract: Endometriosis affects approximately one in 10 women and people assigned female at birth of reproductive age, yet diagnosis is still delayed by years, historically because confirmation required laparoscopy. This review synthesizes which non-invasive tools-expert ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), molecular and microRNA (miRNA) biomarkers, and artificial intelligence (AI)-are ready for clinical use and which have so far been evaluated only in research settings and proposes a pragmatic clinical pathway. This is a narrative review and not a systematic review. Major guidelines now endorse a clinical and imaging-based diagnosis without mandatory laparoscopy. Expert transvaginal ultrasound and MRI identify ovarian endometrioma and deep endometriosis with high specificity and map disease for surgery, but a normal scan does not exclude endometriosis because superficial peritoneal endometriosis remains largely invisible. No blood, urinary, or endometrial biomarker meets criteria for clinical use; circulating miRNA panels have failed independent validation, and a salivary miRNA signature still needs independent, lower-prevalence validation. Radiomics and AI remain investigational pending external validation, calibration, and demonstrated clinical utility. Non-invasive diagnosis is best framed not as one replacement test but as a multimodal, staged pathway in which each tool is used according to how far its evidence has progressed, which shortens diagnostic delay, targets specialist care, and interprets a negative scan safely.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus infection mimicking very early onset inflammatory bowel disease.
abstract: Very early onset inflammatory bowel disease (VEO-IBD), defined as diagnosis before 6 years of age, is often associated with immune dysregulation and monogenic etiologies; however, infectious mimics may be overlooked in low-prevalence regions. We report a 4-year-old male with poor weight gain, intermittent diarrhea, elevated fecal calprotectin, and persistently elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Endoscopy showed diffuse friable colonic mucosa, and biopsies demonstrated focal active colitis with mild crypt distortion. He was diagnosed with VEO-IBD and treated with mesalamine, infliximab, adalimumab, and upadacitinib, with incomplete response. At age 7, he was hospitalized with fever, cytopenias, and pulmonary infiltrates; human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) testing was positive, with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and cytomegalovirus viremia. After discontinuing immunosuppression and initiating antiretroviral therapy, gastrointestinal symptoms and inflammatory markers improved. HIV-associated colitis can closely mimic VEO-IBD, and progressive lymphopenia should prompt evaluation for secondary immunodeficiency.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Treatment of Peripheral Entrapment Mononeuropathies.
abstract: High-resolution neuromuscular ultrasound (US) is a valuable tool for the localization, diagnosis, and provision of conservative treatment to peripheral entrapment mononeuropathies. US-guided interventions require careful coordination of transducer and needle movement along with a detailed understanding of sonoanatomy. Preprocedural planning and positioning are instrumental in performing these interventions and should not be overlooked. Minimally invasive procedures, such as corticosteroid injections, aspiration of ganglia, orthobiologics, and hydrodissection, are useful options for the nonsurgical treatment of mononeuropathies refractory to conservative care. US is effective in determining atypical anatomy such as a bifid median nerve for improved accuracy and safety during injections, and precision based techniques such as hydrodissection may aid in physically separating the nerve from scar tissue and adhesions. The most well researched US guided treatment of entrapment neuropathy is carpal tunnel syndrome which demonstrates promising results from platelet-rich plasma, prolotherapy, hydrodissection, and percutaneous needle release. However, there is significant heterogeneity in procedure technique, injectate composition, injectate volume, and periprocedural conservative care that limits interpretation of the results and warrants continued head-to-head comparisons for research. This review highlights procedural details and outcomes for US-guided interventions of the most well-studied peripheral entrapment neuropathies. Despite many promising findings for these techniques, long-term outcomes and severe nerve compression may still benefit most from surgical decompression.

However, there is significant heterogeneity in procedure technique, injectate composition, injectate volume, and periprocedural conservative care that limits interpretation of the results and warrants continued head-to-head comparisons for research. This review highlights procedural details and outcomes for US-guided interventions of the most well-studied peripheral entrapment neuropathies. Despite many promising findings for these techniques, long-term outcomes and severe nerve compression may still benefit most from surgical decompression.

title: Dual-respiratory-phase low-dose quantitative CT for assessing COPD severity.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the ability of quantitative parameters derived from low-dose dual-respiratory-phase CT to differentiate the severity of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Materials and methods We enrolled 100 COPD patients between October 2023 and October 2024. Inspiratory CT scans were performed using a standard-dose protocol, and expiratory scans were performed using a low-dose protocol. Images were reconstructed with 60% adaptive statistical iterative reconstruction (ASIR). Dual-respiratory-phase image registration was performed on a dedicated "Digital Lung" platform to quantify the following parameters: end-expiratory lung volume (LV EX ), end-inspiratory lung volume (LV IN ), mean lung density at end-inspiration (MLD IN ), mean lung density at end-expiration (MLD EX ), and the mean density ratio (MLD EX/IN ). The percentages of low-attenuation areas (LAA-910% and LAA-950%), emphysema (Emph%), and functional small airways disease (fSAD%) were also calculated. Correlations between CT parameters and pulmonary function were assessed. Significant variables were entered into univariate and multivariate logistic regression models, and a combined predictive model was constructed. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis with internal validation by bootstrap resampling. Results Quantitative parameters, including LV EX , LV IN , LAA-950%, LAA-910%, Emph%, and fSAD%, were significantly correlated with pulmonary function indices (FEV 1 %pred and FEV 1 /FVC; all P < 0.01). Among these, LAA-910% and Emph% showed the strongest correlations with FEV 1 %pred (both r = -0.80). In univariate analysis, LAA-910% demonstrated the highest predictive performance (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.887), followed by Emph% (AUC = 0.884). After adjustment for age and smoking status, multivariate logistic regression identified both Emph% (odds ratio [OR] = 1.298, 95% CI: 1.167-1.488, P < 0.001) and fSAD% (OR = 1.111, 95% CI: 1.040-1.205, P = 0.004) as independent predictors of severe COPD (GOLD 3-4 vs. GOLD 1-2). The combined model incorporating fSAD% and Emph% achieved an AUC of 0.926 (95% CI: 0.883-0.974), with a sensitivity of 80.49% and a specificity of 81.36%. Bootstrap internal validation yielded an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.908, confirming good model generalizability. Conclusion Low-dose expiratory CT combined with dual-respiratory-phase quantitative analysis provides reliable imaging biomarkers that correlate strongly with pulmonary function. The predictive model incorporating both fSAD% and Emph% demonstrates excellent diagnostic performance for assessing COPD severity and may serve as a noninvasive adjunct tool for disease stratification.

title: Deep learning reconstruction in prostate MRI: technical principles, clinical applications, and future directions.
abstract: Multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) has become integral to the detection, localization, risk stratification, and management of prostate cancer. Increasing utilization of prostate MRI in screening, active surveillance, targeted biopsy guidance, and treatment planning has amplified the demand for faster imaging protocols while maintaining high diagnostic quality. Conventional MRI acceleration strategies, including parallel imaging and compressed sensing, improve acquisition efficiency but remain limited by trade-offs involving signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), image sharpness, artifacts, and reconstruction complexity. Deep learning reconstruction (DLR) has emerged as a promising artificial intelligence-based approach for MRI acceleration and image enhancement. Unlike traditional reconstruction methods that rely primarily on predefined mathematical models, DLR uses neural networks to learn image priors and reconstruction features from MRI data. Published studies suggest that DLR may enable accelerated acquisitions while maintaining or, in some settings, improving image quality through denoising, artifact reduction, and improved spatial resolution and lesion conspicuity. However, these effects vary according to the reconstruction algorithm, sequence, acceleration factor, and clinical setting. Variational networks combine physics-based MRI constraints with learned regularization and represent an important framework for DLR. In prostate MRI, available studies have reported substantial reductions in acquisition time for T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted imaging while generally maintaining perceived image quality. Reported benefits include improved lesion conspicuity, reader confidence, and delineation of anatomic structures. Current evidence suggests that DLR generally preserves PI-RADS assessment and diagnostic performance rather than systematically altering lesion categorization; however, evidence demonstrating improvements in diagnostic accuracy or clinical outcomes remains limited. Important limitations include vendor and algorithm dependence, potential reconstruction artifacts, variability in quantitative imaging metrics, limited multicenter validation, and uncertain generalizability across scanners, protocols, and clinical settings. This review summarizes the technical principles underlying DLR, discusses current clinical applications in prostate MRI, highlights representative studies and workflow implications, reviews limitations, and outlines future directions for this rapidly evolving technology.

title: A Clinical Algorithm for Gynecomastia: From Diagnosis to Surgical Management.
abstract: Background Gynecomastia is a heterogeneous disorder spanning the full pediatric-to-adult age range; however, comprehensive single-institution analyses that integrate endocrine, comorbid, drug-related, and surgical perspectives within one framework remain limited. We characterized the demographic and etiologic landscape of gynecomastia in a large retrospective cohort, propose a practical diagnostic algorithm derived from these patterns, and summarize the institutional experience with surgical management. Methods We retrospectively reviewed all male patients with an electronic-medical-record diagnosis of gynecomastia at two tertiary academic hospitals between January 2011 and March 2026. True gynecomastia was confirmed clinically and, where indicated, by ultrasonography, mammography, or magnetic resonance imaging. Patients were categorized by primary etiology (physiologic, drug- or substance-induced, endocrine, pathologic systemic, or idiopathic) using a standardized diagnostic workflow, and surgical candidates were graded according to the Simon classification. Results Of 754 patients screened, 562 met criteria for true gynecomastia (pediatric ≤ 17 years, 30 [5.3%]; adult ≥18 years, 532 [94.7%]; mean age 58.7 ± 19.8 years; median 64, range 0-95). Bilateral disease accounted for 75.9% of patients with documented laterality. Idiopathic disease was the largest category (362; 64.4%), followed by drug- or substance-induced disease (135; 24.0%), pathologic systemic disease (43; 7.7%; predominantly chronic liver and kidney disease), endocrine disorders (13; 2.3%), and overt physiologic gynecomastia (6; 1.1%). Spironolactone (71 patients; 52.6% of drug-induced cases) and antiandrogen / androgen-deprivation therapy agents (28; 20.7%) jointly accounted for nearly three quarters of drug-induced disease. Etiologic distribution differed markedly by age: physiologic and idiopathic causes predominated in adolescents, whereas drug-induced disease rose sharply from the fifth decade onward and accounted for ≈26-29% of cases in patients aged 50-80 years. Forty-three patients (7.7%) underwent surgical correction (mean age 33.7 ± 18.9 years), most commonly for long-standing persistent disease or cosmetic and psychosocial indications; surgical conversion was substantially higher in idiopathic (9.3%) than in drug-induced (2.2%) or systemic pathologic disease (2.3%). Histopathology confirmed benign glandular hyperplasia in all 43 surgical specimens; no occult male breast carcinoma or other malignant tissue was identified (0 of 43), and patients with male breast carcinoma at initial presentation were excluded a priori. Conclusions Across a 15-year cohort, idiopathic and drug-induced disease (chiefly spironolactone and antiandrogen-class agents) accounted for nearly 90% of adult cases. A stepwise algorithm based on examination, medication review, and selective endocrine and radiologic testing classified etiology in routine practice, and surgery matched to Simon grade remained the definitive treatment for long-standing, severe, or psychosocially distressing disease. Level of evidence iii This journal requires that authors assign a level of evidence to each article. For a full description of these Evidence-Based Medicine ratings, please refer to the Table of Contents or the online Instructions to Authors www.springer.com/00266 .

title: VERIDAH: solving enumeration anomaly-aware vertebra labeling across imaging sequences.
abstract: Objectives Although the identification of enumeration anomalies has potential clinical implications for chronic back pain and operation planning, the thoracolumbar junction is poorly assessed and rarely described in clinical reports. Additionally, even though multiple deep-learning-based vertebra labeling algorithms exist, there is a lack of methods to automatically label enumeration anomalies. Materials and methods We introduce "Vertebra Identification with Anomaly Handling" (VERIDAH), a novel vertebra labeling algorithm based on multiple classification heads combined with a weighted vertebra sequence prediction algorithm. We use the NAKO dataset for MRI and a CT cohort to retrospectively evaluate the labeling performance by computing how often the model is correct in predicting the vertebra labels, including enumeration anomalies. Statistical significance was assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results On 1000 T2w sagittal (mean age 52 ± 11, 52% female) and 365 CT (mean age 74 ± 21, 44% female) images, we show that our approach surpasses existing models on T2w TSE sagittal (98.30% vs. 94.24% of subjects with all vertebrae correctly labeled, p < 0.01) and CT imaging (99.18% vs. 77.26% of subjects with all vertebrae correctly labeled, p < 0.01) and works in arbitrary field-of-view images. VERIDAH correctly labeled the presence of thoracic enumeration anomalies in 87.80% and 96.30% of T2w and CT images, respectively, and lumbar enumeration anomalies in 94.48% and 97.22% for T2w and CT, respectively. Conclusion VERIDAH offers enumeration anomaly robust vertebra labeling in CT and T2w sagittal imaging and is publicly released along with a spine segmentation model. Key points QuestionAutomatically identifying enumeration anomalies in the spine is important in determining the correct vertebra labels, especially in limited field-of-view imaging. FindingsA carefully designed classifier with multiple classification heads and a sequence predictor provides superior results on large benchmarks, both in CT and MRI. Clinical relevanceThe proposed method identifies vertebra levels even in very limited field-of-view imaging, and correctly predicts enumeration anomalies, making downstream tasks such as surgery planning easier. Its public availability enables studies and applications to take these spinal anomalies into account.

title: Accuracy of general-purpose large language models (LLMS) in interpreting adolescent idiopathic scoliosis radiographs: a comparative study with experienced spine surgeons.
abstract: Purpose This study evaluates the accuracy of general-purpose, vision-capable large language models (LLMs) in interpreting adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) radiographs and compares their outputs with an expert surgeon consensus reference standard. Methods This retrospective comparative diagnostic accuracy study analyzed 128 anonymized AIS radiographic case sets from 128 different patients, including standing coronal and sagittal radiographs and lateral bending films. ChatGPT GPT-5.2 Instant, Gemini 3 Flash, and Grok 4.1 were evaluated through their official web interfaces in January 2026 using the original standardized prompt based on the Lenke classification system. Model inputs were de-identified raw radiographs without measurement lines, Cobb values, vertebral labels, or Surgimap overlays. Three spine surgeons with more than 10 years of deformity surgery experience independently assessed all cases using Surgimap. Surgeon consensus was the reference standard. title: Acute management of pelvic ring injuries: identifying common treatment principles across institutional algorithms.
abstract: Introduction Pelvic ring injuries are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, particularly in patients presenting with hemodynamic instability and major hemorrhage. Numerous institutions have developed management algorithms for the acute treatment of pelvic ring injuries; however, the common principles underlying these pathways remain unclear. Methods A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched on January 8, 2026, for peer-reviewed publications published from January 1, 2006, through December 31, 2025 that described algorithms, pathways, or protocols for the acute management of pelvic ring injuries. Two independent reviewers performed study selection and data extraction. Algorithm components related to mechanical stabilization, physiologic assessment, imaging, hemorrhage control, and damage control resuscitation were extracted and compared using descriptive quantitative and qualitative synthesis. Results The search identified 328 records that underwent title and abstract screening, and 63 articles were assessed for full-text eligibility. Twenty-five studies were included in the final analysis. All included algorithms (25/25, 100%) used physiology-based decision-making. Early noninvasive mechanical stabilization was specified in 23/25 algorithms (92%); pelvic binders were specified in 17/25 (68%). Angiography with potential angioembolization was included in 19/25 algorithms (76%), exploratory laparotomy in 10/25 (40%), and resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) in 3/25 (12%). Computed tomography was incorporated into 20/25 algorithms (80%), whereas pelvic radiography was included in 18/25 (72%). Fracture morphology was used as a treatment decision point in 4/25 algorithms (16%), and pelvic packing was described in 20/25 publications (80%). Conclusion Published algorithms for the acute management of pelvic ring injuries demonstrate substantial consistency despite institutional variation. Early mechanical stabilization, physiologic assessment, damage control resuscitation, radiologic evaluation, and structured hemorrhage-control pathways were identified as the most common components of contemporary management algorithms.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonist use and contrast-associated acute kidney injury after contrast-enhanced CT and CT angiography in adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease: a propensity score-matched cohort study.
abstract: Aims To examine whether glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) use is associated with contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI) after contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CE-CT) or computed tomographic angiography (CTA) in adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Methods We conducted a TriNetX retrospective cohort study of adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD who underwent CE-CT or CTA from January 2020 to January 2025. GLP-1 RA use was defined by a prescription within six months before imaging. The primary outcome was a new acute kidney injury diagnosis within three days. Separate 1:1 propensity score-matched analyses were conducted for CE-CT and CTA, with eGFR-stratified and sensitivity analyses. Results After matching, the CE-CT and CTA cohorts included 6,995 and 3,285 pairs, respectively. CA-AKI occurred in 3.8% of GLP-1 RA users versus 4.5% of non-users after CE-CT (odds ratio [OR] 0.84, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.71-0.99) and in 4.5% versus 6.1% after CTA (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.59-0.92). The absolute risk differences were 0.7% points and 1.5% points, respectively. HbA1c remained imbalanced after matching. Negative-control outcomes were null, and eGFR-stratified associations were inconsistent between cohorts. Conclusions GLP-1 RA use was associated with a lower observed risk of CA-AKI after CE-CT and CTA in adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD. Residual HbA1c imbalance and the observational design limit causal interpretation; prospective studies using creatinine-based outcomes are needed.

title: Diagnosis of Suspected Pituitary Microadenomas: The Complementary Role of Habitat-based Non-enhanced MRI Radiomics Features.
abstract: To develop and validate a combined model for detecting pituitary microadenomas in suspected cases using non-contrast T1-weighted sagittal (T1SAG) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and to assess its performance as a non-contrast imaging-based tool for clinical decision support.This retrospective two-center study enrolled 519 patients with suspected pituitary microadenomas, divided into a training set (n = 321), an internal validation set (n = 80), and an external test set (n = 118). Radiomics features were extracted from both the entire pituitary gland and its habitat subregions, generated via unsupervised K-means clustering. Eight predictive models were constructed using logistic regression: a clinical model, an intra-pituitary radiomics model, three individual habitat models (Habitat 1, 2, and 3), an early-fusion model combining all habitats, an ensemble model integrating the probability outputs of the three habitat models, and a combined model that integrated clinical, intra-pituitary, and the optimal fusion model. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curves (ROC), calibration curves, and decision curve analysis.Among all models, the combined model demonstrated the best predictive performance across all three cohorts, achieving areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.885 (95% CI: 0.850-0.920) in the training set, 0.788 (95% CI: 0.690-0.885) in the internal validation set, and 0.796 (95% CI: 0.712-0.880) in the external test set. The combined model also achieved the highest accuracy and sensitivity across all datasets.The combined prediction model showed robust performance in distinguishing pituitary microadenomas in suspected cases, offering enhanced clinical decision support while reducing dependence on contrast-enhanced MRI examinations.

title: Evaluating Explicit Anatomical Priors Beyond a Mature CT Detector for Six Acute Abdominal Emergencies.
abstract: To test whether anatomical priors from a general-purpose organ segmentation model (TotalSegmentator, TS), applied at inference or during training, improve an externally validated YOLOv11 detector for six acute abdominal emergencies. The frozen detector was applied to 827 external Stanford Merlin CT studies with language-model report labels; a nested 280-study radiologist-adjudicated subset was the reference standard. TS-derived slice selection (Arm A), organ-state integration (Arm B), and their combination (Arm C) were compared with the detector alone under frozen, recalibrated, and fine-tuned conditions. The detector was also retrained from scratch (identical 10-epoch budget) with image channels only, with the patient's TS organ maps as added input channels, or with another patient's maps. AUROC was primary; comparisons used a paired study-level bootstrap. The detector generalized externally (macro AUROC 0.816 cohort; 0.879 adjudicated). Slice selection was non-inferior but not beneficial: nearly all confident detections already lay within the anchored organ's axial range; organ-state fusion improved AUROC only for cholecystitis (hypothesis-generating). In single runs, training with organ maps raised internal test mAP@0.5 (0.517 versus 0.482), and the model depended on the maps, but external macro AUROC did not improve (0.822 versus 0.829; Δ -0.007, 95% CI -0.019 to +0.007) and kidney-stone AUROC fell (0.678 versus 0.768; exploratory), unlike with another patient's maps. Per-site recalibration was the most effective operating-point adjustment (macro F1 +0.021); annotation-free fine-tuning reduced discrimination. Explicit anatomy, applied after detection or during training, did not improve this detector's overall external discrimination. Per-site recalibration gave the largest operating-point gain.

title: Investigation on Automatic Classification of Bone, Lymph Node, and Local Lesions in CT Images of Prostate Cancer Patients.
abstract: Accurate assessment of different types of prostate cancer (PCa) lesions is a crucial part of treatment planning. Following a computed tomography (CT) or a positron emission tomography (PET)/CT imaging scan, a significant amount of time is required from the clinicians to detect lesions and characterize them by their anatomical locations. To facilitate the development of new image analysis applications, we investigated the potential of automated classification of PCa lesions between bone metastases, lymph node metastases, local lesions, and other PCa lesions in CT images via machine learning (ML) and deep learning models. We annotated a total of 4949 PCa lesions by their type in a private dataset of 18 F-prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT images of 532 PCa patients and an external test set of publicly available PSMA PET/CT images from 30 patients. Using information of coordinates of the detected lesions, we automatically extracted 15 different features from the CT and the results of the automated 3D anatomical segmentation tool TotalSegmentator for each lesion, and trained several traditional ML models to classify lesions by their anatomical type. Additionally, we experimented with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) of different dimensionalities with CT and TotalSegmentator inputs. According to our results, the most accurate model was XGBoost with an overall accuracy of 96.0%. It identified bone metastases, lymph node metastases, and local lesions with sensitivities of 97.9±1.2%, 95.2±1.3%, and 93.1±2.8% in the five-fold cross-validation experiments of the primary data and 96.3%, 94.0%, and 80.0% on the external test set, respectively. Conversely, the CNNs underperformed the best ML models in distinguishing local lesions. To conclude, a simple ML model can accurately classify PCa lesions between bone, lymph node, and local lesions based on CT images, lesion locations, and automated anatomical segmentation data, but more research is required for distinguishing PCa lesions outside these categories.

title: Building and Validating a Data-Governance Workflow for Artificial Intelligence-Based Tuberculosis Detection from Chest Radiographs, and Quantifying the Impact of Data Leakage.
abstract: Studies applying artificial intelligence (AI) to tuberculosis (TB) detection from chest radiographs (CXR) focus on models and metrics, yet the quality, provenance and reproducibility of the data workflow decide the reliability of results; duplicate images and non-patient-level splitting inflate evaluation metrics. We propose a seven-step data-governance workflow: multi-source standardisation, provenance management, three-hash deduplication (MD5, pHash, dHash), patient-level splitting, invariant-check auditing, lung segmentation and version freezing by data fingerprint. Four leakage scenarios (deduplication on or off; patient-level or random split) were repeated 20 times with paired splits and compared with the clean scenario on per-repeat differences. On 46,410 CXR images from seven public sources, the workflow removed duplicates at file and content level, standardised 16,554 TB Portals DICOM images, generated 34,554 lung masks without failure and sealed every layer with SHA-256 hashes. On the three-class multi-source corpus, the area under the curve (AUC) saturated near 0.997 in every scenario, consistent with source-class confounding; paired leakage effects were statistically detectable but below 0.1 percentage points. On a single-source probe task (drug resistance within TB Portals), random image-level splitting inflated the internal AUC by 1.7 percentage points (95% confidence interval 0.9 to 2.4; p = 0.001), or 1.2 points after a deduplication gap found during revision was repaired; in a holdout design, an internal gap of 1.1 points shrank to 0.4 points on a patient-disjoint holdout. The magnitude of leakage depends on data structure and must be measured; a rigorous governance workflow makes that measurement, and data reuse, verifiable.
originalAbstract: Studies applying artificial intelligence (AI) to tuberculosis (TB) detection from chest radiographs (CXR) focus on models and metrics, yet the quality, provenance and reproducibility of the data workflow decide the reliability of results; duplicate images and non-patient-level splitting inflate evaluation metrics. We propose a seven-step data-governance workflow: multi-source standardisation, provenance management, three-hash deduplication (MD5, pHash, dHash), patient-level splitting, invariant-check auditing, lung segmentation and version freezing by data fingerprint. Four leakage scenarios (deduplication on or off; patient-level or random split) were repeated 20 times with paired splits and compared with the clean scenario on per-repeat differences. On 46,410 CXR images from seven public sources, the workflow removed duplicates at file and content level, standardised 16,554 TB Portals DICOM images, generated 34,554 lung masks without failure and sealed every layer with SHA-256 hashes. On the three-class multi-source corpus, the area under the curve (AUC) saturated near 0.997 in every scenario, consistent with source-class confounding; paired leakage effects were statistically detectable but below 0.1 percentage points. On a single-source probe task (drug resistance within TB Portals), random image-level splitting inflated the internal AUC by 1.7 percentage points (95% confidence interval 0.9 to 2.4; p = 0.001), or 1.2 points after a deduplication gap found during revision was repaired; in a holdout design, an internal gap of 1.1 points shrank to 0.4 points on a patient-disjoint holdout. The magnitude of leakage depends on data structure and must be measured; a rigorous governance workflow makes that measurement, and data reuse, verifiable.

title: Abdominal Ultrasound Simulation from Semantic Labels Using Paired Label-to-Physics-Based Image Translation.
abstract: Purpose Current abdominal ultrasound (US) simulation methods often require CT-based anatomical references for ray-casting, limiting deformation, and pathology variability. We propose a learning-based pipeline trained to predict physics-based images derived from CT scans from semantic labels, enabling controlled simulations without patient-specific CT volumes at inference time. Methods We introduce a two-stage pipeline that maps anatomical segmentations to realistic US images through a simplified US image. Stage I synthesizes this image from semantic labels using models trained on CT-based ray-casting outputs. Stage II refines it into a realistic US scan using anatomically guided unpaired translation. Deformations and pathologies are generated by editing anatomical maps. Results We evaluated Pix2Pix and the Semantic Diffusion Model (SDM) in Stage I, followed by segmentation-guided CycleGAN (SG-CycleGAN) refinement in Stage II. SDM significantly outperformed Pix2Pix in morphological metrics, including MAE ↓ (19.85 vs. 21.65), SSIM ↑ (0.28 vs. 0.24), and mIoU ↑ (0.43 vs. 0.29), whereas Pix2Pix yielded better perceptual point estimates (LPIPS ↓ : 0.17 vs. 0.19; FID ↓ : 0.32 vs. 0.37; KID ↓ : 0.25 vs. 0.48). Conclusion Training paired generative models with physics-based supervision enables approximation of CT-derived ray-casting outputs at inference time directly from semantic labels. Although the pipeline does not require patient-specific CT volumes at inference time, CT-derived segmentations and ray-casting simulations remain necessary to train Stage I. Once trained, the framework enables controllable healthy and pathological simulations through semantic map modification.

title: The role of low muscle strength in predicting mortality in patients with liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Sarcopenia is a prevalent complication in chronic liver disease (CLD), traditionally assessed by muscle mass. Recent paradigm shifts focus to dynapenia as the primary determinant of adverse outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the role of dynapenia, as measured by handgrip strength (HGS) and ultrasound-derived diaphragmatic excursion, in predicting mortality in this population. This prospective study included consecutive outpatients with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma history attending a tertiary hepatology unit. Muscle mass was assessed in subgroups using bioimpedance analysis (BIA) and computed tomography (CT). Associations between sarcopenia proxies and 24-month all-cause mortality were analyzed with adjusted Cox regression models, and survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier curves. Ninety-one patients were included (age 73.4 ± 8.1 years; 71 [78%] male); 20 (22%) had dynapenia. Twenty-two deaths occurred at two years (24.2%). Over 24 months, dynapenia (by HGS) and diaphragmatic excursion were associated with mortality in adjusted models (aHR 1.68, 95% CI 1.12-2.53, p = 0.012; aHR 0.58, 95% CI 0.34-0.97, p = 0.042). In subgroups, they remained the only muscle parameters associated with mortality, while muscle mass indices were not significant. Finally, Kaplan-Meier estimates showed lower 24-month survival in dynapenic patients across groups (in overall population 65% vs. 79%, p = 0.05). Low muscle strength is a key prognostic parameter in patients with cirrhosis and HCC. In our small cohort, it was the only muscle-related measure significantly associated with mortality. These findings support further evaluation of muscle strength assessment as a potential tool for risk stratification in this population.

title: Yolo-c2ecasa: a lightweight attention-enhanced model for three-class brain tumor localization and classification in MRI.
abstract: Brain tumor localization and type classification in MRI are important tasks in computer-aided medical image analysis. However, achieving competitive localization and classification performance with lightweight models remains challenging because reducing model complexity may weaken feature representation and localization ability. In this paper, we propose YOLO-C2ECASA, a lightweight attention-enhanced object detection framework based on YOLOv11 for three-class tumor localization and classification in tumor-positive MRI images. The present study focuses on glioma, meningioma, and pituitary tumors and does not address tumor-versus-no-tumor screening. The proposed C2ECASA module replaces the original self-attention design with a parameter-efficient spatial-channel attention mechanism. It integrates improved channel attention, lightweight spatial attention, C2-based feature preservation, and adaptive fusion to enhance lesion-relevant feature representation with limited computational cost. The proposed model was compared with representative object detection models. In the single-run comparison with representative object detectors, YOLO-C2ECASA maintained competitive detection performance while requiring only 2.4M parameters, 6.2G FLOPs, a model size of 5.01 MB, and a GPU inference time of 1.9 ms per image. More importantly, across ten independent runs under scratch initialization, YOLO-C2ECASA achieved mean mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 values of [Formula: see text] and [Formula: see text]. Under pretrained initialization, the corresponding repeated-run results were [Formula: see text] and [Formula: see text], respectively. Under CPU-only deployment, YOLO-C2ECASA achieves an inference time of 27.4 ms per image, further demonstrating its feasibility for resource-constrained environments. These results indicate that the proposed model achieves competitive detection performance while maintaining a lower computational cost than the compared detectors. Ablation and repeated-run experiments further demonstrate that the complete C2ECASA configuration achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated configurations while maintaining low computational complexity. Overall, the proposed method provides a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for lightweight brain tumor localization and type classification in tumor-positive MRI images.

title: Ultra-High Gradient Thin-Slice Oblique Coronal Zoomed DWI for Perihilar and Distal Cholangiocarcinomas: Improved Tumor Depiction for Precise Surgical Planning.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Accurate preoperative assessment of extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (eCCA) remains challenging with conventional imaging. This study aimed to investigate the value of thin-slice oblique coronal zoomed diffusion-weighted imaging (OC-Z-DWI) on an ultra-high gradient system for eCCA (including both perihilar and distal subtypes) assessment. Materials and methods This prospective study enrolled 93 patients with pathologically diagnosed eCCA (54 males, 66.8 ± 9.0 years; 62 perihilar and 31 distal) and 43 patients without eCCA (19 males, 62.9 ± 11.8 years). All patients underwent conventional magnetic resonance imaging and OC-Z-DWI on an ultra-high gradient system (200 mT/m amplitude). Image quality of OC-Z-DWI was evaluated, and diagnostic performance and lesion sizing were compared between the conventional protocol and one incorporating OC-Z-DWI. Results OC-Z-DWI showed good scoring in noise, artifacts, and overall image quality (mean 3.83 ± 0.41, 3.65 ± 0.56, and 3.80 ± 0.43, respectively). Adding OC-Z-DWI to the conventional protocol significantly improved lesion edge sharpness (3.89 ± 0.31 vs 3.60 ± 0.53, P < 0.001), lesion conspicuity (3.94 ± 0.25 vs 3.75 ± 0.46, P < 0.001), diagnostic confidence (3.86 ± 0.38 vs 3.58 ± 0.65, P < 0.001), and diagnostic performance (AUC 0.917 vs 0.869, P = 0.018). Lesion size measurements with the OC-Z-DWI-based protocol demonstrated strong pathological correlation (r = 0.822), with lower pathological-imaging diameter discrepancy than the conventional protocol (median 4.0 mm vs 7.0 mm, P < 0.001). These improvements were consistent across both perihilar and distal subgroups. Furthermore, R0 resection patients exhibited a stronger imaging-pathology sizing correlation than R1 patients (r = 0.891 vs 0.528, P = 0.021). Conclusion Ultra-high gradient thin-slice OC-Z-DWI provides high-quality images for eCCA characterization. Adding OC-Z-DWI to the conventional magnetic resonance protocol enhances lesion delineation, diagnostic performance, and tumor sizing accuracy, delivering more precise preoperative information to optimize surgical planning.

title: Retrospective Lung-RADS v2022 Characterization of Fatal Lung Cancer Cases in the National Lung Screening Trial.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Persistent lung cancer mortality despite screening is multifactorial. Characterizing computed tomography (CT) findings preceding fatal lung cancer may identify imaging features and screening challenges that warrant further study. Materials and methods We conducted a retrospective, outcome-enriched case series nested within the 26,722-participant low-dose computed tomography arm of the National Lung Screening Trial. Among 359 participants who died of lung cancer within the prespecified interval, exclusions for positive baseline screening (n = 186), incomplete screening (n = 28), withdrawal/declined screening (n = 19), unavailable CTs (n = 6), or three negative screens followed by death 2+ years after the final screen (n = 29) yielded 91 participants. Screening CTs were retrospectively assessed using the Lung Imaging Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) v2022. Four thoracic radiologists independently reviewed visible-in-retrospect nodules and adjudicated whether they met criteria for suspicion. Results Of 91 participants, 22 (24%; 95% confidence interval (CI), 17%-34%) had visible-in-retrospect nodules considered suspicious under Lung-RADS v2022 ("missed"), 16 (18%; 95% CI, 11%-27%) had visible nodules not meeting suspicion criteria ("not callable"), 50 (55%; 95% CI, 45%-65%) had no visible-in-retrospect nodule, and 3 (3.3%) were inconclusive. Missed nodules were frequently juxtapleural (41%), obscured (50%), or irregularly bordered (68%); not-callable nodules were frequently <6 mm (75%), juxtapleural (56%), or irregularly bordered (56%). Conclusion In this selected fatal-case series, small and juxtapleural nodules were common among visible nodules not meeting Lung-RADS v2022 suspicion criteria. These findings warrant evaluation in representative screening populations and should not be interpreted as estimates of population-level Lung-RADS performance.

Materials and methods

We conducted a retrospective, outcome-enriched case series nested within the 26,722-participant low-dose computed tomography arm of the National Lung Screening Trial. Among 359 participants who died of lung cancer within the prespecified interval, exclusions for positive baseline screening (n = 186), incomplete screening (n = 28), withdrawal/declined screening (n = 19), unavailable CTs (n = 6), or three negative screens followed by death 2+ years after the final screen (n = 29) yielded 91 participants. Screening CTs were retrospectively assessed using the Lung Imaging Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) v2022. Four thoracic radiologists independently reviewed visible-in-retrospect nodules and adjudicated whether they met criteria for suspicion.

Results

Of 91 participants, 22 (24%; 95% confidence interval (CI), 17%-34%) had visible-in-retrospect nodules considered suspicious under Lung-RADS v2022 ("missed"), 16 (18%; 95% CI, 11%-27%) had visible nodules not meeting suspicion criteria ("not callable"), 50 (55%; 95% CI, 45%-65%) had no visible-in-retrospect nodule, and 3 (3.3%) were inconclusive. Missed nodules were frequently juxtapleural (41%), obscured (50%), or irregularly bordered (68%); not-callable nodules were frequently <6 mm (75%), juxtapleural (56%), or irregularly bordered (56%).

Conclusion

In this selected fatal-case series, small and juxtapleural nodules were common among visible nodules not meeting Lung-RADS v2022 suspicion criteria. These findings warrant evaluation in representative screening populations and should not be interpreted as estimates of population-level Lung-RADS performance.

title: A multimodal MRI radiomics sonata for differentiating small renal masses: a two-center retrospective study.
abstract: Background Accurately distinguishing benign from malignant small renal masses (SRMs) is crucial to avoid unnecessary surgeries, yet reliable preoperative diagnostic tools remain limited. Methods A total of 189 patients with SRMs from two hospitals (2018-2022) were enrolled. Clinical data and MRI features were analyzed by two radiologists. Radiomics features were automatically extracted from manually segmented ROIs using dedicated software. Significant features were selected via univariate analysis, multivariate regression, and Lasso to develop three models: radiomics, clinical, and combined nomogram. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using the Area Under the receiver operating characteristic Curve (AUC). Results The radiomics-clinical nomogram was constructed using T2WI signal intensity (p < 0.001), pseudocapsule (p = 0.001), and radiomics score (Rad-score, p = 0.001) via multivariate logistic regression. In the training set, the nomogram achieved an AUC of 0.962 (95% CI: 0.931-0.993), outperforming both the radiomics model (AUC = 0.918, 95% CI: 0.862-0.974) and the clinical model (AUC = 0.856, 95% CI: 0.780-0.933). Favorable performance was observed in the internal validation set (nomogram: AUC = 0.981, 95% CI: 0.944-1.000; radiomics model: AUC = 0.912, 95% CI: 0.750-1.000; clinical model: AUC = 0.844, 95% CI: 0.578-1.000) and external validation set (nomogram: AUC = 0.971, 95% CI: 0.886-1.000; radiomics model: AUC = 0.928, 95% CI: 0.841-0.989; clinical model: AUC = 0.916,95% CI: 0.760-0.976). Conclusion All three models enable effective and non-invasive preoperative differentiation of benign from malignant SRMs, with the radiomics-clinical nomogram exhibiting the highest diagnostic accuracy, supporting its potential as a valuable clinical tool.

title: Dual-state adaptive unrolled network for structure-preserving low-dose CT image restoration.
abstract: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces spatially heterogeneous noise and artifacts that can obscure subtle anatomical structures. We address post-reconstruction image-domain LDCT restoration, where degradation suppression and structure preservation impose competing demands on a single restoration trajectory. We propose DSAUNet, a Dual-State Adaptive Unrolled Network that maintains persistent anatomy- and degradation-oriented latent states across unrolled stages. Rather than acting as transient feature branches, the evolving states participate in parameterizing subsequent restoration behavior through a degradation-oriented global policy coordinate for stage-level modulation and state-derived confidence variables for spatially selective regulation. Direction-aware prior modeling and multi-scale state guidance further realize this state-parameterized restoration process. Under the reported protocols, DSAUNet achieves 40.3721 dB PSNR and 0.9642 SSIM on 2DeteCT, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.6320 dB and 0.0108, and achieves 47.4277 dB PSNR and 0.9846 SSIM under the patient-level five-fold Mayo evaluation, with a 1.0920 dB PSNR gain over the strongest PSNR baseline. On LoDoPaB-CT, it further obtains 38.5501 dB PSNR and 0.9141 SSIM, with the best PSNR, SSIM, and VIF among the compared methods. Controlled raw-state, persistent state-swapping, policy-coordinate, and confidence-map analyses support functionally differentiated state roles and active adaptive regulation. Bidirectional 2DeteCT-Mayo zero-shot experiments reveal direction-dependent transfer behavior, while unified profiling characterizes an accuracy-complexity trade-off. Together, these results support persistent dual-state controlled unrolling as a structured approach to image-domain LDCT restoration within the evaluated settings.

title: A robust biomarker combining radiomic and CA19.9 information to predict distant relapse-free survival after radiochemotherapy in pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Background The radiomic feature Statistical Percentile 10% (p10%), extracted from [¹⁸F]FDG-PET images, has been previously identified and validated as a robust predictor of distant progression-free survival (DPFS) in unresectable pancreatic cancer (LAPC). This study aimed to maximize its prognostic potential by combining p10% with CA19.9 serum levels and assessing its generalizability across distinct clinical settings. Methods We analyzed 287 LAPC patients treated with chemoradiotherapy (CRT) and a validation cohort of 72 patients enrolled in the CASSANDRA trial (resectable/borderline-resectable PDAC). Cox models combined p10% with CA19.9 levels measured before RT in LAPC patients, and before surgery for CASSANDRA patients. Results p10% was independently prognostic in both cohorts and its integration with CA19.9 significantly improved the prediction. In the LAPC cohort, the combined model achieved C-index=0.71, with median DPFS of 4.0-vs-15.0 months (p<0.0001;HR=3.22). In the pre-surgery setting (CASSANDRA trial), the model showed good rank-order discrimination (C-index=0.65), with median survival of 11.6 months vs not-reached (p=0.0018). However, the calibration slope of 0.54 suggests that absolute risk prediction requires recalibration in the surgical cohort. Conclusions Integrating p10% with CA19.9 provides a broader representation of tumor aggressiveness. The combined biomarkers demonstrate consistent performance across different disease stages supporting their use for treatment personalization.
